idiom_name: traits + match/isInstanceOf probing; scala.Selectable for lookup-based member access
implementation_notes: Scala traits are interfaces with implementations, so an extension contract is a trait, and additive growth of a shipped trait is non-breaking because concrete members carry their own implementations - the preservation half comes for free. Runtime negotiation is the JVM probe (match on the extension trait or isInstanceOf/asInstanceOf), and supplying an extension for a foreign type is idiomatic through implicit conversions or givens that adapt a legacy object to the required trait, at the cost of implicit-scope discipline. Scala 3 makes lookup-based extension a language feature: extending scala.Selectable with selectDynamic(name: String) turns obj.word into a dynamic selection resolved at run time (applyDynamic for calls), optionally checked structurally when the expected type carries a refinement; scala.reflect.Selectable is the reflection-backed implementation and inherits the limits of reflective access.
code_sketch:
component match
  case ta: TextAccessor => ta.words.foreach(check)
  case _               => ()

final class Record(pairs: (String, Any)*) extends Selectable:
  private val fields = pairs.toMap
  def selectDynamic(name: String): Any = fields(name)   // record.words via lookup
pitfalls: isInstanceOf/asInstanceOf are erased for generic types: List[Int] and List[String] are indistinguishable, so a probe can succeed and the cast fail later.
Lookup-based members (Selectable, scala.Dynamic) have no static existence proof unless the expected type carries a refinement; typos become runtime failures and reflective selection is slow.

Implicit conversions used to supply capabilities are scope- and version-sensitive (Scala 3 givens, language.implicitConversions warnings), so an adaptation can silently stop applying after an import change.
A match with a default branch always compiles, so the compiler never proves that every subject's extensions are handled.
